title: Evaluating a Deterministic-Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 intent→configuration tasks, cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1) to test whether a guarded pipeline—single-shot LLM generation (gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution (planned episodes 600, completed 600, model_calls_used 301) produced baseline = 299/300 valid configurations (99.667%) and guarded = 300/300 valid configurations (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.00333; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Confirmatory secondary hypothesis H2 (repair recovery among initially invalid outputs): initially invalid = 1, repaired = 1 → point estimate 1.0 (100%); 95% Clopper–Pearson CI = [0.025, 1.0]. The preregistered H1 (≥50% relative reduction) is not supported because baseline performance was near‑ceiling and the recorded runtime sampling semantics (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference. We report the preregistered design, execution accounting, and archived validator/repair traces, and discuss statistical and methodological implications for future, more challenging evaluations.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configurations is central to intent‑driven NetOps but misordered or incorrect changes can cause outages and security regressions. Recent surveys and system demos recommend generate→verify→repair architectures that combine LLM generation with deterministic validators or simulators and, where appropriate, human approval. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory experiment to quantify whether a minimal guarded pipeline—a frozen deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to unguarded single‑shot generation. Our contribution is: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation (N=300) with deterministically generated intent→configuration tasks, (2) full archival of model outputs, validator traces, and repair traces, and (3) an evidence‑grounded analysis of statistical and methodological factors (notably sampling semantics and baseline ceiling effects) that affect detectability of practical safety gains.
sections.related_work: Work on LLM‑assisted intent translation and configuration generation demonstrates promising lab results but highlights safety risks from hallucination, missequencing, and overconfidence. Cross‑domain studies show retrieval augmentation and verifier/repair loops improve grounding; architecture papers for NetOps increasingly advocate deterministic validators as floor‑safety nets. However, rigorous preregistered A/B experiments measuring concrete misconfiguration‑rate reductions from a minimal validator+single‑repair pipeline in NetOps are sparse. Our experiment positions itself within this gap by providing a preregistered paired test and publishing deterministic validator and repair traces to enable reproducible scrutiny.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and hypotheses: The run followed preregistration cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1. Confirmatory hypotheses were: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus plain single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. Design and sampling: paired within‑task design with 300 deterministic task seeds produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; each pair had a baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded arm (same initial candidate validated with deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and ≤1 automated repair call). The execution contract set initial_generation_calls_per_task=1 and maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1. Model/runtime metadata: declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini; execution/model_configuration.json records generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" and temperature = null. We explicitly note that a null temperature by itself is not authoritative about paired sampling; the archived generation_semantics field is the authoritative runtime control that caused reuse of the same sampled candidate across both arms for each task, thereby increasing within‑pair correlation. Scoring and estimand: validator produced binary pass/fail per task; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact McNemar (α=0.05). All raw responses, per‑task validator traces, repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts were archived.
sections.results: Execution accounting (archived): planned episodes = 600, completed episodes = 600, complete pairs = 300, model_calls_used = 301, provider call audit stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 300, repair: 1}. Primary outcomes (archived analysis artifacts): baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%); paired contingency: n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.00333; paired bootstrap (percentile) 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Repair usage and H2: the guarded pipeline invoked the single permitted repair call once and corrected the sole initially invalid configuration. Thus initially invalid = 1 and repaired = 1 → repair recovery point estimate = 1.0 (100%); 95% Clopper–Pearson CI = [0.025, 1.0]. The preregistered H1 (≥50% relative reduction) is not supported because baseline performance was near‑ceiling and the shared_initial_candidate sampling semantics reduced available discordant pairs and therefore statistical sensitivity to the preregistered effect size.
sections.discussion: Three operationally relevant lessons follow. First, ceiling effects: when baseline single‑shot generation already attains near‑perfect validity on a synthetic task bank, even a perfect deterministic safety net yields little measurable relative improvement; experimental designs must align preregistered effect sizes and power calculations to plausible baseline error rates. Second, sampling semantics and paired designs interact: reusing a shared initial candidate per pair (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") isolates validator corrective power but raises within‑pair correlation and can shrink discordant counts used by McNemar, reducing inferential power; future preregistrations should predefine whether paired arms draw independently or reuse the same candidate and adjust power planning accordingly. Third, repair evidence: the single repair call in this run successfully recovered the only failure (H2: 1/1), but the small denominator yields a wide Clopper–Pearson interval [0.025,1.0], underscoring the need for larger counts of initial failures (via harder or adversarial tasks) to estimate repair effectiveness precisely. Methodological implications: to evaluate operational readiness for autonomous change execution, future experiments should (a) use harder/adversarial task suites, (b) broaden validator fidelity (including emulation or dynamic checks), (c) permit multi‑iteration repair, (d) vary sampling semantics (independent draws vs shared), and (e) include multiple model families.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=300) using gpt‑5‑mini and a frozen deterministic validator with ≤1 automated repair iteration, baseline single‑shot generation was near‑ceiling (299/300) and the guarded pipeline produced 300/300 valid outputs; a single repair call corrected the sole observed failure but did not yield a statistically detectable improvement for the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis. We explicitly report H2: the repair recovered 1/1 initially invalid outputs (100%; 95% Clopper–Pearson CI = [0.025,1.0]). The run highlights that task difficulty, sampling semantics, validator coverage, and baseline error rates jointly determine whether guarded pipelines produce detectable safety gains in confirmatory designs. We release full archived artifacts (model responses, validator/repair traces, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts) to support reproducibility and to inform follow‑on experiments that probe harder operational regimes.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

Near‑ceiling baseline performance (299/300) removed headroom to detect the preregistered target effect (≥50% relative reduction); shared_initial_candidate sampling semantics further reduced discordant pairs and statistical sensitivity.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair-success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → point estimate 1.0) yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
